pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: You write a program as text in a file. Why can't the CPU run that file directly, and what has to happen before it can run?
expected_points: the CPU only executes machine code — number-encoded instructions wired into the chip
source code is text designed for humans, not something the CPU understands
it must be translated to machine code, by a compiler ahead of time or an interpreter while running

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a compiler and an interpreter? Give one language for each.
expected_points: a compiler translates the whole program ahead of time into an executable file of machine code
an interpreter is a program that reads and performs the source itself, piece by piece, on every run
Go (or C, Rust) is compiled; Python (or JavaScript) is interpreted

questions.prompt: While a program is running, what is the CPU's job and what is memory's job? What two kinds of things live in memory?
expected_points: the CPU executes tiny instructions one at a time, extremely fast, tracking which instruction is next
memory is the fast workspace of numbered boxes the program uses while it runs
memory holds both the program's instructions and its data
memory is not the disk — disk keeps files permanently, memory is wiped when the program ends

questions.prompt: You run a compiled program and the word Hello appears on screen. Walk me through what happened in between, step by step.
expected_points: the operating system finds the executable on disk
it loads the machine code into memory, sets aside memory for data, and points the CPU at the first instruction
the CPU fetches and executes instructions one at a time
an instruction hands the text to the operating system, which puts it on the screen; the program then exits and its memory is reclaimed

questions.prompt: You misspell a name in your code. In a compiled language versus an interpreted one, when do you find out — and why does that follow from how each works?
expected_points: compiled: at compile time, because the compiler checks the whole program before producing an executable
interpreted: often only when the interpreter reaches that line at run time
the timing difference is a direct consequence of whole-program-ahead-of-time versus piece-by-piece-while-running

questions.prompt: When you executed the paper-machine program by hand, were you acting as a compiler or an interpreter? Why?
expected_points: an interpreter — reading one instruction at a time and performing it immediately
a compiler would have translated the whole program into another form first, without performing it
